chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Abu Jamilah, from Humran, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him).

From a man who made a bequest at the time of his death saying: 'Free so-and-so, and so-and-so, and so-and-so,' until he mentioned five. The third of his estate was evaluated, but it did not reach the value of the eight slaves he ordered to be freed. He said: 'They are valued, and the third is considered; then the first named is freed, then the second, then the third, then the fourth, then the fifth. And if the third is insufficient, that applies to those he named last, because he bequeathed after the third's limit what he does not own and which is not permissible for him.'"

And the narrations we mentioned earlier regarding bequest of more than the third, with the existence of heirs, carry another meaning: that the heirs were only granted and born after he had made the bequest. For if that is the case, the bequest is valid in its entirety or in what he bequeathed, even if it is more than the third.

And that which indicates this is what he narrated: -(789) 21 - Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Mutatabbib wrote to him: 'And afterwards, may Allah prolong your life, we inform you, O our master, that we are in doubt regarding this bequest which Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Darayab bequeathed - and that is that the freedmen of our master and his righteous slaves mentioned that it is not for the deceased to bequeath if he has a son more than a third of his wealth, and Muhammad ibn Yahya had bequeathed - more than half of what he left from his estate. If our master and our lord, may Allah prolong his stay, sees fit to open the concealment of this darkness which we complained about and explain that to us, we will act upon it, if Allah the Exalted wills.'
So he (peace be upon him) answered: 'If he bequeathed it before he had a son, his bequest is valid, and that is because his son was born after him.'
And the relied-upon opinion is what we mentioned first, and what we mentioned adds clarification that the bequest is not valid in what exceeds the third.

What he narrated: -(790) 22 - Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf said: Muhammad ibn Al-Hasan ibn Abi Khalid had a slave boy who was sound, known, called Maymun. When death approached him, he bequeathed to Abu Al-Fadl Al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf all his inheritance and estate, saying: 'Make it dirhams and send them to Abu Ja'far al-Thani (peace be upon him).' He left a wife who was pregnant, brothers who had entered Islam, and a Zoroastrian mother.

He said: So I did what he bequeathed, gathered the dirhams, and delivered them to Muhammad ibn Al-Hasan. My mind inclined to write to him explaining what he bequeathed to me and what the deceased left from heirs. So Muhammad ibn Bashir and others from our companions advised me not to write the explanation, as I would not need it, for he would know that without my explanation. But I refused except to write to him with that, upon his right and truthfulness. So I wrote, collected the dirhams, and delivered them to him (peace be upon him).
So he ordered him to set aside from it the third, deliver it to him, and return the remainder to his executor, who returns it to his heirs.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on bequeathing more than one-third of one's estate in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the Shia jurisprudential principle that a bequest (*wasiyyah*) is generally limited to one-third of the estate to protect heirs' rights, yet it remains valid in full if the testator made it before the birth of his heirs. It further details the proportional distribution mechanism when multiple beneficiaries are named but the one-third share is insufficient, prioritizing them by the order of mention. This ruling underscores the balance between the testator's autonomy and the mandatory inheritance shares (*fara'id*) preserved in Shia law.
